narrative: Star Vetter automatically searches for eclipsing binary stars in data from the TESS satellite. When two stars orbit each other, they periodically eclipse and dim the light we receive. Our pipeline identifies candidates by analyzing light curves for statistically significant dimming patterns, then cross-checks them against six established variable-star catalogs to flag novel systems. Each candidate survives a contamination check and undergoes an automated pixel-level examination to confirm the signal comes from the target star itself rather than nearby objects. So far we have confirmed 186 candidates from 12,825 sampled targets. To support this work, we trained a machine learning model on nearly 1,900 labeled examples; it provides a second opinion on candidate quality and outperforms our rule-based baseline. Not all candidates are free of caveats, but the multi-stage vetting process substantially raises confidence that confirmed systems are real eclipsing binaries worth further study.

faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary star?
faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a system of two stars orbiting each other in a plane we view edge-on from Earth. As they orbit, each star periodically moves in front of the other from our perspective, blocking some of its light. This causes the total brightness to dip in a regular, repeating pattern. By studying these dips (eclipses) in the light curve, astronomers can infer the sizes, temperatures, and orbital properties of the stars.

faqs.question: What do you mean by 'candidate' versus 'confirmed'?
faqs.answer: A candidate is a target showing an eclipse-like signal in its light curve that has passed statistical tests and is novel (not already in known variable-star catalogs). A confirmed candidate is one that has passed the pixel-level check, an automated test that verifies the signal comes from the target star itself and not from nearby contaminating sources. Confirmed does not mean the system has been independently verified by other observers or spectroscopic follow-up.

faqs.question: What is the machine learning screening score?
faqs.answer: We trained a machine learning model (gradient boosting) on 1,894 labeled examples to assign a quality score to candidates. The model outperforms our baseline rule-based approach. However, it is a second opinion only. Currently, every candidate that passes statistical vetting and the novelty cross-match is sent to pixel-level checking regardless of the ML score. The ML model is not used to gate or filter which candidates get checked.

faqs.question: How does a candidate get checked at the pixel level?
faqs.answer: The pixel-level check is a fully automated process. It examines the spatial distribution of the signal across pixels in the image to confirm that the eclipse signature originates from the target star and not from a nearby star or other contaminating source. Candidates that pass this test are marked as confirmed on our site.

faqs.question: What if the eclipse period looks aliased?
faqs.answer: We perform an odd/even eclipse-depth test: we compare the depths of odd-numbered eclipses to even-numbered eclipses. If the period is misidentified (aliased), these depths will typically differ. Candidates showing consistent eclipse depths across odd and even cycles are more likely to have the correct period. Candidates flagged as potentially aliased carry a note on their individual pages.

faqs.question: Can I verify a result myself?
faqs.answer: Yes. TESS data and light curves are public. You can download the data for any confirmed candidate listed here and examine the light curve yourself using freely available software. This allows independent observers to assess the signal quality and eclipse properties.

faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it is listed on this site?
faqs.answer: Being listed on Star Vetter as confirmed is the endpoint of our automated pipeline. We do not perform radial-velocity spectroscopy, conduct follow-up observations, submit results to scientific journals, or add systems to official catalogs. The site serves as a catalog of candidates for community use; what researchers choose to do with these systems is up to them.
